To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the visual system can be trained to respond to a new visual feature (a new visual object), and that this training is accompanied by a change in the functional organization of the visual system.

1) a 180 degree rotation of a cat's eye causes a complete inversion of the visual hemifield seen by that eye; 2) the inversion is complete and permanent, with no tendency for the cat to recover from it; 3) the inversion is due to a reversal of the retinal image, not to a change in the direction of gaze; and 4) the inversion is not accompanied by any change in visual behaviour.
the brain can learn to represent the world as a single image, even when it is exposed to two different images.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the development of the visual system and its plasticity in the adult, with the aim of understanding how the brain develops and how it is capable of modifying its structure and function in response to environmental changes.
understanding the mechanisms by which visual information is processed in the brain.
the development of the visual cortex and the mechanisms underlying the development of the retinotectal projection.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the visual system of the cat is organized in terms of retinotectal and retinocortical maps.
the cat cortex is not capable of developing an orderly representation of the retina in a topographic manner.
the visual cortex is not a homogeneous unit and that its organization is a function of the experience of the animal.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
it is possible to produce a new cortical representation of the visual world by training the visual system of a young animal.
the brain does not use a retinotopic map to interpret visual space.
the brain has a mechanism for determining the directions of objects, and that this is based on the retinotopic maps.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the visual system has an innate bias to interpret the world in a certain way, even if the world is not as the system expects it to be, and that this bias is reflected by a change in the way the visual system processes the information it receives.
the brain is not a passive recipient of sensory input.
we need to think about these maps not just as a representation of the visual field but also as a representation of how we move in that space.
